original-passage-0135ed8f8e471127a501.passage_text: Rohan volunteered to carry a box of costumes to the school hall. On the way, he saw a younger pupil looking for a lost notebook. Rohan could not search while holding the large box, and he knew the costumes were needed soon. He took the box directly to the hall and asked another volunteer to help the pupil search. When he returned, the notebook had been found beneath a bench. The pupil thanked both of them. Rohan had initially felt that leaving the search meant refusing to help. Seeing the result, he realised that asking the right person could be useful assistance too.

original-passage-e61fbe708891c20af994.passage_text: The painter covered a wall with a pale morning sky. Before she could finish the birds, evening sunlight turned the colours warm. She stepped back, displeased that the light had changed what she had planned. A boy standing nearby said the unfinished shapes looked like leaves caught in a breeze. The painter looked again. She did not erase the sky or declare the boy correct. She sketched one clear bird among the remaining shapes and returned the next morning to see the wall in the light for which she had first designed it.

original-passage-c661bea9b68ff7abe06d.passage_text: Dev kept score during a friendly cricket match. As the players packed their bags, he noticed that he had counted one run twice. Correcting it would turn his team's victory into a tie. He showed the scorebook to the captains, who checked the recorded deliveries and agreed on the correction. One teammate said nobody would have noticed. Dev answered that noticing it himself was enough reason to check. The captains changed the result without replaying the match. On the walk home, Dev felt disappointed about the lost victory but relieved that the scorebook now matched the game.

original-passage-0c5cbbed83a8f6a1c585.passage_text: For years, the brass bell above the shop door had announced every visitor. When it cracked, the shopkeeper fitted a quieter bell. His daughter liked being able to hear a conversation without interruption. He still turned towards the door before the new bell rang, expecting the old sound. One evening, he placed the cracked bell beside the till rather than returning it to the doorway. A customer lifted it gently and recognised its worn handle. The shopkeeper smiled. The old bell could remain part of the shop without being required to do its former work.

original-passage-bd9ef81cc82883c1bb47.passage_text: Amina practised a speech until she could recite every sentence. On the morning of the competition, the organiser shortened each speaker's time. She tried to speak faster, but the words became hard to follow. Her teacher asked which idea she most wanted the audience to remember. Amina removed an anecdote and two examples, retaining the central argument and one supporting example. She finished within the new limit. Afterwards, she missed the anecdote she had enjoyed writing, yet she could explain why it had been removed. The shorter speech preserved her purpose even though it did not preserve every sentence.

original-passage-7e691ebb38511efbe5f9.passage_text: The station clock had stopped at ten past four. Each morning, travellers looked up, checked their watches and continued towards the platform. The tea seller never corrected the clock; it was beyond his reach. One afternoon, a child asked whether the trains had stopped too. He pointed to a train sliding past the far platform. Its windows caught the sun one after another. The child watched until it disappeared, then looked back at the clock. For the first time that day, the tea seller noticed the contrast himself: the hands stood still above a place where almost everything was moving.

original-passage-cce6a78aa3f6ad864be0.passage_text: Meera unfolded a paper boat her brother had left on the windowsill. Beneath the creases she found the drawing they had used to make it: a house, two crooked trees and a sun almost hidden at the edge. She considered flattening the sheet completely, but the folds resisted. Instead, she opened only enough to see the drawing and set it beside a photograph. The boat no longer stood upright. The picture was not smooth either. In the evening light, both forms remained visible, neither restored exactly to what it had been before.

original-passage-d60c3db784308a4460d8.passage_text: A fictional repair club allocated its weekly budget to tools and replacement parts. Members initially proposed buying a new drill. The inventory check then showed that an existing drill worked but lacked a charging cable, while several repairs were waiting for inexpensive switches. The club bought the cable and switches instead. This allowed it to resume the waiting repairs without exhausting the budget. The minutes explained that the decision concerned the club's immediate needs; they did not claim that buying new equipment was always wasteful. Members agreed to reconsider the drill purchase if the repaired equipment could no longer handle their workload.

original-passage-cd55b65c95234040105a.passage_text: Rain had washed the chalk game from the lane. The children arrived with fresh chalk and began drawing again. One child remembered the old squares as longer; another insisted that the turning square had been on the left. They argued until a passing neighbour asked whether the new game had to reproduce the old one. After a moment, they drew a wider turning square in the middle. Their feet soon covered the fresh lines with pale dust. From her doorway, the neighbour could no longer tell which marks belonged to yesterday and which belonged to the game they had just invented.

original-passage-0640bfac6d71f74032be.passage_text: A fictional community centre offered a beginner's pottery workshop and a more advanced workshop. Registration for the advanced session required completion of the beginner's session or a short demonstration of equivalent skills. An experienced visitor who had never attended the centre passed the demonstration and joined the advanced group. Another visitor chose the beginner's session after finding the demonstration difficult. The organiser explained that the alternative routes recognised prior experience while checking readiness for the work. Attending a particular earlier course was one way to qualify, rather than the only acceptable evidence of the relevant skills.

original-passage-249ea78da59fc5fa63d1.passage_text: In a fictional exhibition, visitors received either a printed map or a map containing the same information with larger lettering. Volunteers recorded how often each group asked for directions. Those receiving the larger lettering asked less often. The organisers noted that volunteers had handed out the maps on different days, when different galleries were open. They proposed a second trial in which both versions would be distributed on the same day. Meanwhile, both maps remained available. The first trial provided a reason to investigate readability, but it could not separate the effect of lettering from differences between the days.

original-passage-92b547616ba401788f58.passage_text: A fictional garden committee published a watering roster on a noticeboard. When a volunteer could not attend, that person was asked to arrange a replacement and update the board. After two missed sessions, the committee learned that replacements had been arranged but the board had not been changed. Other volunteers therefore believed the slots were empty and duplicated the work. The committee added a simple confirmation step: the replacement would initial the revised slot. The adjustment addressed the recording of responsibility rather than imposing an additional watering session. The report did not attribute the duplication to volunteers being unwilling to help.

original-passage-3a3e89358b7611f2f96f.passage_text: In this fictional report, a school canteen tested two ways of reducing disposable cups. During the first week, a sign asked students to bring their own cups. During the second, the canteen also lent washable cups against a refundable deposit. Disposable-cup use fell in both weeks, with a larger fall in the second. However, attendance was lower during the second week because one class was away. The report therefore recommended comparing cups used per student before attributing the larger fall to the lending scheme. It also recorded that most borrowed cups were returned. The trial suggested a possible benefit, while leaving the size of that benefit uncertain.

original-passage-62c765944064a26e2c5b.passage_text: At a rehearsal, Nisha played a melody more quickly than the rest of the group. She thought the faster pace made it exciting. Their conductor asked everyone to listen while one drummer kept a steady beat. Nisha noticed that the flute's quieter phrases disappeared when she rushed. During the next attempt, she waited for the drummer's beat and heard the phrases clearly. Afterwards, a classmate praised the performance. Nisha said that she had changed very few notes. What she had changed was the space she gave the other players. She kept her faster version for a solo rehearsal later.

examples.passage_text: A Maharatna Company, Indian Oil Indian Oil is India’s largest commercial organisation. It is the top ranked Indian company in the Fortune ‘Global 500’ listings (2017). Indian Oil’s vision is driven by a group of dynamic leaders, who have made it a name to reckon with. With an over 34,000 strong workforce, a Maharatna Company, Indian Oil has been helping to meet India’s energy demands and reaching petroleum products in every part of India for over five decades.  It plans to increase its business operations all around the world.  The company plans to invest ₹ 20,000 crore in 2017 – 18 acquisitions and plans to expand overseas. The company is always believed to be ahead of the demand. Last year too, IOC had invested close to ₹ 20,000 crore, including around ₹ 16,000 crore in various Indian projects and on acquisition for upstream in Russia.  The company believed that if the goals are well defined, employees are aware of what the organisation has to do and what they must do to achieve those goals.  Changes or events cannot be eliminated, but they can be anticipated and managerial responses to them can be developed. Policy formation serves as the basis of coordinating the activities and efforts of different divisions, departments and individuals.  It helps in avoiding confusion and misunderstanding. Manager can look into the future and make a choice from amongst various alternative courses of action.
examples.explanation: The case concerns setting future goals and planned action, identifying planning. Official key: 4 (D).

examples.passage_text: India had an independent economy before the advent of the British rule. Though agriculture was the main source of livelihood for most people, yet, the country’s economy was characterised by various kinds of manufacturing activities. India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc. These products enjoyed a worldwide market based on the reputation of the fine quality of material used and the high standards of craftsmanship seen in all imports from India. The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy. Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into a supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain. Obviously, the colonial government never made any sincere attempt to estimate India’s national and per capita income. Some individual attempts which were made to measure such incomes yielded conflicting and inconsistent results. Among the notable estimators — Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao and R.C. Desai — it was Rao, whose estimates during the colonial period were considered very significant. However, most studies did find that the country’s growth of aggregate real output during the first half of the twentieth century was less than two per cent coupled with a meagre half per cent growth in per capita output per year.
examples.explanation: NCERT describes precolonial strengths in textiles, metal, and precious-stone work, supporting option C. Official key: 3.

examples.passage_text: India had an independent economy before the advent of the British rule. Though agriculture was the main source of livelihood for most people, yet, the country’s economy was characterised by various kinds of manufacturing activities. India was particularly well known for its handicraft industries in the fields of cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone works etc. These products enjoyed a worldwide market based on the reputation of the fine quality of material used and the high standards of craftsmanship seen in all imports from India. The economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India were concerned more with the protection and promotion of the economic interests of their home country than with the development of the Indian economy. Such policies brought about a fundamental change in the structure of the Indian economy — transforming the country into a supplier of raw materials and consumer of finished industrial products from Britain. Obviously, the colonial government never made any sincere attempt to estimate India’s national and per capita income. Some individual attempts which were made to measure such incomes yielded conflicting and inconsistent results. Among the notable estimators — Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao and R.C. Desai — it was Rao, whose estimates during the colonial period were considered very significant. However, most studies did find that the country’s growth of aggregate real output during the first half of the twentieth century was less than two per cent coupled with a meagre half per cent growth in per capita output per year.
examples.explanation: NCERT gives aggregate output growth below two per cent and per-capita growth about half a per cent yearly, option D. Official key: 4.

When I was in my late teens and still undecided about which language I should write in, he told me that the language one is born into, one’s mother tongue, can be the only possible medium of creative expression. For most of his life, my father, Sripat Rai, had been a Hindi editor and critic. Off and on, he translated writings into English from Hindi. He was fond of saying that a failed writer becomes a critic. The weight of his literary expectation came, eventually, to rest on me. He seemed happy that I was showing an inclination for writing. “She will go far,” he told my mother after reading the first story that I sent him from Melbourne. My father’s pronouncement on the mother tongue stayed with me when I later started writing fiction in Hindi. Another thing that I barely acknowledged even to myself was that I felt something like shame whenever I thought of writing in English. It seemed wrong for a granddaughter of Premchand even to be thinking so. Our family had a certain linguistic pride. I knew that Premchand was famous, but I had not at that time realised the extent of his popularity. The fact that I was the granddaughter of Premchand, followed me everywhere. Everyone had a story to tell about their personal engagement with his fiction — the shopkeeper, the long time cook in my father’s Delhi house, a tea vendor, etc. The list was long, for there was practically no one who had not read something by him that had moved them. However, it was this very ubiquity, the reverence and love that he inspired in people, that made of him something too large for me to comprehend in the early years of my life. It led also to the strange feeling that, without having read him and just by being related to him, I had somehow inhaled his writing. The reading happened much later.

PAGE 1
 
 
For the Year 2026 
 
  
Accountancy / Book 
Keeping – 301                     
Syllabus for CUET 
(UG)
 
 

PAGE 2
 
1 | P a g e   
Unit I:  Accounting for Partnership  
• Nature of Partnership Firm:  Partnership deed (meaning, importance).  
• Accounts of Partnership:  Fixed v/s Fluctuating capital, Division of profit among partners, 
Profit and Loss Appropriation account, guarantee of profit to a partner, past adjustments. 
 
Unit II:  Reconstitution of a Partnership firm 
• Changes in profit sharing ratio among the existing partners – Sacrificing ratio and Gaining 
ratio.  
• Accounting for Revaluation of Assets and reassessment of Liabilities and Distribution of 
reserves and accumulated profits.  
• Goodwill: Nature, Factors affecting and Methods of valuation: Average profit, Super profit 
and Capitalisation methods.  
• Admission of a Partner: Effect of admission of partner, Change in profit sharing ratio, 
Accounting treatment for goodwill, Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities , 
Reserves adjustment/distribution of (accumulated profits) and adjustment of capitals.  
• Retirement/Death of a Partner: Change in profit sharing ratio, Accounting treatment of 
goodwill, Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities, Adjustment of Accumulated 
profits (Reserves) , Preparation of deceased partner’s  capital account and his executor’s 
account, Preparation of Loan Account. 
 
Unit III:  Dissolution of Partnership Firm  
• Meaning, Settlement of accounts: Preparation of Realisation Account and related Accounts 
(excluding piecemeal distribution, sale to a company and insolvency of a Partner). 
  
Unit IV:  Company Accounts: Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital 
• Features and type of companies. 
• Share Capital: Meaning, Nature and Types 
• Accounting for Share Capital: Issue and Allotment of Equity and Preference Shares; Over 
subscription and Under subscription; Issue at par  and premium; Calls in advance, Calls in 
arrears, Issue of shares for consideration other than cash.  
• Accounting treatment of Forfeiture of Shares and Re-issue of forfeited shares.  
• Presentation of shares capital and Debentures in company’s balance sheet. 
• Issue of Debenture – At par, premium and discount; Issue of debentures for consideration 
other than cash.  Issue of debentures with terms of redemption, Debenture as collateral 
security- concept, Interest on debentures, writing off discount/Loss on issues of debenture. 
 
 
 
 
 

PAGE 3
 
2 | P a g e   
 
 
Unit V:  Analysis of Financial Statements  
• Financial Statements of a Company : Preparation of simple financial statements of a 
company in the prescribed form with major headings and sub headings. 
• Financial Analysis: Meaning, Significance, Purpose and Limitations.  
• Tools for Financial Analysis: Comparative statements, Common size statements.  
• Accounting Ratios: Meaning and Objectives and types:   Liquidity Ratio, Solvency Ratio, 
Activity Ratio, Profitability Ratio. 
• Cash Flow Statement: Meaning and Objectives, Preparation, Adjustments related to 
depreciation, amortization, dividend and tax, purchase and profit or loss  on sale of non-
current assets (as per revised standard issued by ICAI).  
 
Optional to Unit V 
 
Unit V:  Computerised Accounting System  
• Overview of Concept and Types of Computerised Accounting System (CAS). 
• Features of a Computerised Accounting System, Advantages, limitations 
• Structure of a Computerised Accounting System:  chart of accounts, Codification and 
Hierarchy of account heads. 
• Accounting information system (AIS).  
• Accounting Applications of Electronic Spreadsheet. 
• Features offered by Electronic Spreadsheet. Applications of Electronic Spreadsheet in 
generating accounting information, preparing reports using pivot Table, common errors in 
spreadsheet, depreciation schedule, loan repayment schedule, payroll accounting.  
• Graphs and Charts in electronic spreadsheet for Business Data.

Unit I:  Nature and Significance of Management

• Coordination – nature and importance.

• Principles of Management – meaning, nature and significance. 
• Fayol’s principles of management. 
• Taylor’s Scientific Management – Principles and Techniques.

• Business Environment – meaning and importance. 
• Dimensions of Business Environment – Economic, Social, Technological, Political and Legal. 
 
Unit IV:  Planning 
• Meaning, features, importance, limitations. 
• Planning process. 
• Types of Plans – Objectives, Strategy, Policy, Procedure, Method, Rule, Budget, Programme. 
 
Unit V: Organising 
• Meaning and importance.

• Formal and informal organisation. 
• Delegation: meaning, elements and importance. 
• Decentralization: meaning and importance. 
• Difference between delegation and decentralisation.

• Selection – meaning and process. 
• Training and Development – meaning, need, methods – on the job and off the job methods of 
training.

types, factors determining choice of channels.

promotion and public relation, Role of Advertising, objections to Advertising.
